blocks.content: A daemon is a process specifically designed to run in the background, with no interactive terminal attached and no user sitting there watching it, typically started once at boot and left running indefinitely to provide some ongoing service. Every web server, SSH server, and scheduled job runner on a real Linux system is, underneath, exactly this kind of process.

This chapter ties together several threads from earlier in this module, fork, exec, and specifically the double fork orphaning pattern from the orphan processes chapter, into the concrete, standard recipe real Unix daemons actually use to detach themselves fully from wherever they were originally started.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409298372-792916857.png
1. What Makes a Process a Daemon
blocks.text: 1. What Makes a Process a Daemon

blocks.content: A daemon is defined less by what code it runs and more by how it relates to the rest of the system. It has no controlling terminal, meaning there is no interactive terminal session it is attached to and could receive terminal generated signals like SIGINT from. It typically runs continuously, started once, often at boot, and kept running indefinitely rather than executing once and exiting.

Its parent process is typically init or systemd, PID 1, exactly the universal adopter described in the orphan processes chapter, since a properly detached daemon has deliberately orphaned itself away from whatever process originally launched it.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A daemon is a process deliberately detached from any controlling terminal, running continuously in the background under the supervision of init or systemd rather than an interactive user.
2. Familiar Real World Examples

Daemons are not an obscure or rare category, they run constantly on essentially every real Linux system, usually invisible unless something goes wrong. sshd listens for and handles incoming SSH connections. cron wakes up periodically to run scheduled jobs. syslogd collects log messages from across the system and writes them somewhere durable. A web server like nginx runs as a daemon, serving requests indefinitely with no terminal attached at all.

3. The Double Fork, Revisited

The orphan processes chapter already introduced the double fork pattern as the classic way to deliberately create a fully independent, orphaned process. This chapter builds directly on that: the double fork is not just an interesting side effect of process management, it is the actual first concrete step of turning an ordinary program into a real daemon.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409298373-914776818.png

Forking once and letting the original process exit immediately accomplishes something specific worth calling out clearly: it guarantees the resulting process is not the session leader of whatever terminal session it was started from, which matters directly for the very next step.
4. The Full Detachment Sequence

Turning a process into a proper, well behaved daemon follows a well established sequence of steps beyond just the initial fork, each one severing one more remaining connection back to the terminal or environment it was originally started from.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409298373-119580502.png
setsid: truly detaching from any terminal
blocks.text: setsid: truly detaching from any terminal

blocks.content: After the first fork, the resulting process calls setsid, which makes it the leader of a brand new session with no controlling terminal associated with it at all. This is the step that actually guarantees the daemon can never accidentally receive a terminal generated signal like SIGINT or SIGHUP meant for whatever terminal session it originated from.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409298373-587108897.png
blocks.alt: setsid: truly detaching from any terminal

blocks.content: Changing the working directory

A long running daemon typically changes its working directory to the file system root. Leaving it pointed at some other directory, on a removable or unmounting file system, could otherwise prevent that file system from ever being cleanly unmounted while the daemon keeps running indefinitely.
5. Handling stdin, stdout, and stderr

A daemon with no controlling terminal has nowhere meaningful for its standard input, output, or error streams to actually go if left pointed at wherever they originally were. Writing to stdout in a process with no attached terminal generally means that output is simply lost, going nowhere useful at all.

The standard fix is redirecting all three standard streams, typically closing stdin entirely since a daemon should never expect interactive input, and redirecting stdout and stderr to a dedicated log file or to the system logging facility, syslog, so that meaningful output is preserved and reviewable later rather than silently discarded.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409298373-766187346.png
6. Modern Practice: Letting systemd Handle It
blocks.text: 6. Modern Practice: Letting systemd Handle It

blocks.content: On modern Linux systems, application authors increasingly do not need to manually implement the full double fork and detachment sequence by hand at all. systemd, the standard init replacement on most current distributions, provides its own well defined mechanism, a unit file, describing how to start, stop, restart, and supervise a service, with systemd itself handling the process lifecycle management directly.

This does not make the underlying concepts in this chapter obsolete, systemd itself still relies on the same fork and exec and process management primitives underneath, and understanding the manual sequence remains genuinely important both for interviews and for working with systems or tools that still expect a program to daemonize itself the traditional way.

7. The Full Daemon Lifecycle

Pulling every piece of this module together, a typical daemon lifecycle looks like this: the system boots, init or systemd starts the daemon, either through the daemon own manual detachment sequence or through systemd own service management, the daemon runs indefinitely in the background providing its service, and it eventually stops only when explicitly signaled, typically with SIGTERM, tying directly back to the signals chapter, giving it a chance to shut down cleanly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394737-136133292.png
8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming any background process, started for instance by appending an ampersand in a shell, is automatically a proper daemon, when a genuine daemon specifically detaches from its controlling terminal entirely, not just runs asynchronously from that same terminal session.","Forgetting to redirect standard output and error streams, silently losing important log output that a real daemon needs preserved somewhere durable.","Believing systemd has made the underlying fork, exec, and orphaning concepts obsolete, when systemd itself is built directly on top of exactly those same primitives."]
items: Assuming any background process, started for instance by appending an ampersand in a shell, is automatically a proper daemon, when a genuine daemon specifically detaches from its controlling terminal entirely, not just runs asynchronously from that same terminal session.
Forgetting to redirect standard output and error streams, silently losing important log output that a real daemon needs preserved somewhere durable.
Believing systemd has made the underlying fork, exec, and orphaning concepts obsolete, when systemd itself is built directly on top of exactly those same primitives.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to walk through the full manual daemonizing sequence from memory, fork, exit the parent, setsid, change directory, redirect standard streams, and explain why each individual step is necessary, not just recite them as an unexplained checklist.
